claims.text: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr is a refractory high-entropy alloy.
Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition as a function of temperature.
The cast/HIPed, homogenized, and slow-cooled condition has a continuous ordered B2 matrix with discrete BCC precipitates.
The continuous-B2 condition is brittle and has low room-temperature ductility.
Solutionizing at 1400 °C for 20 minutes followed by water quenching produces a weakly ordered BCC structure containing nanometer-scale B2 regions.
Subsequent annealing at 600 °C for 120 hours followed by water quenching produces an inverted microstructure with a continuous disordered BCC matrix and discrete approximately 50 nm B2 precipitates.
The relevant structural mediator is the continuity and distribution of ordered B2 relative to disordered BCC.
The ordered B2 phase is inherently brittle.
A continuous B2 matrix suppresses dislocation motion, thereby causing low ductility.
Replacing the continuous B2 matrix with a continuous disordered BCC matrix enhances dislocation mobility and produces high ductility.
Discrete nanoscale B2 precipitates provide precipitation strengthening.
Elevated temperature activates competing slip systems that produce anomalous strengthening.
A weakly ordered BCC structure with nanoscale B2 regions has substantially greater room-temperature compressive ductility than the continuous-B2 condition.
The fully inverted continuous-BCC/discrete-B2 condition has high room-temperature ductility.
At approximately 600 °C, the inverted microstructure has a higher yield strength than at room temperature while retaining significant ductility.
The cited study performed uniaxial compression tests at 25 °C and 600 °C at an initial strain rate of 0.001 s^-1.
Temper embrittlement is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but normally absent from high-entropy alloys.
A ductile–brittle–ductile transition can be deliberately generated in this high-entropy alloy through microstructural control.
The proposed transition occurs between room temperature and approximately 600 °C and depends on processing parameters and phase fractions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes a ductile–brittle–ductile transition with temperature, but the intervention creates brittle and ductile states through different processing routes, and the predicted outcome is ductile at both room temperature and 600 °C for the inverted microstructure. No brittle intermediate-temperature state for a single fixed microstructure is specified.
